WASHINGTON, Nov 18 : A federal grand jury has indicted a Russian national on charges of acting as a foreign agent to target the technology and defense company Palantir and surveil its employees, according to court documents and two people familiar with the matter. Working with Russian collaborators, Igor D'iu allegedly traveled from Russia and stalked employees of what the Justice Department described in its affidavit and press release only as a Silicon Valley technology and defense company. Two people familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, identified the company as Palantir Technologies Inc, which has a large office in Palo Alto, California but is based in Florida.  D'iu took photos of employees' computer screens while at a coffee shop near company offices, according to the affidavit. He also followed a female staff member nearly 30 miles (50 km)  but stopped his pursuit after the employee contacted the police, prosecutors said.

“The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company’s assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia,” Craig H. Missakian, the top federal prosecutor in San Francisco, said in a statement. Palantir CEO Alex Karp has publicly backed Ukraine, and the company has said it deployed its technology to the country. Palantir did not respond to a request for comment. Russia's embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment. One of the people, who is familiar with the company's thinking, said the attempted breach was unsuccessful and will not change the company's support for Ukraine. The person added that Palantir is unlikely to be the only technology and defense company targeted by the Russians. News of the alleged surveillance comes amid heightened scrutiny of tech company security after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned in the wake of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of having Chinese intelligence ties. D'iu, who is being held in federal custody, is charged with two counts related to his alleged work as a Russian agent, one count of interstate stalking and one count of fraud related to identification documents. He faces up to 21 years in prison. Reuters could not immediately determine if he had appointed a lawyer.  Bloomberg first reported that Palantir was the target of the Russian surveillance campaign.  D'iu allegedly entered the United States through the Texas-Mexico border in July and searched for company employee addresses online in August, according to the indictment. After following two employees on consecutive days out of the company's Palo Alto offices in early September, he was contacted by local law enforcement. FBI agents later found a falsified US passport, Russian passports, roughly $18,000 in cash and 10 handwritten addresses, at least five of which were linked with employees' home addresses. Prosecutors said his co-conspirators told him he was working for "the Motherland" and directed him to set up his computer near the tech company's offices so they could try to obtain information from nearby employees.  He is next scheduled to appear in court on Tuesday.

A United States House panel asked Microsoft on Wednesday (Nov 18) to brief lawmakers on a report which said the company could allow the Chinese firm ByteDance to use OpenAI models through Microsoft's Azure cloud platform. Technology news outlet The Information reported that Microsoft was nearing a US$500 million deal with ByteDance. The chairman of the House Select Committee on China, John Moolenaar, said the panel wanted more details "given serious concerns over American companies helping China catch up to the US in the AI race". "Microsoft takes misuse of its AI services seriously and is committed to enforcing its terms of service, complying with applicable laws, and honouring its partner agreements," a Microsoft spokesperson said, adding that the company does not comment on confidential customer negotiations.

Anthropic's IPO raised US$81.31 billion on Wednesday (Nov 18), eclipsing SpaceX’s offering to claim the title of the largest stock-market debut on record. Anthropic said the IPO was priced at US$83 apiece, above its previously targeted range and valuing the company at approximately US$1.5 trillion. Reuters was first to report that the IPO was upsized by about 19 per cent to 980 million shares from its initial plan to sell 825 million shares at between US$70 and US$78 apiece.  Anthropic is also raising US$26 billion through a private placement at the IPO price, the filings show.

On a fully diluted basis, the IPO values the company at about US$1.5 trillion, including securities such as stock options and restricted stock. On a non-diluted basis, the valuation stands at about US$1.1 trillion. Anthropic, the first major frontier artificial-intelligence model developer to do an IPO, follows SpaceX's June offering, as investors jump at the chance for exposure to the fast-growing industry, even as the industry also faces mounting questions over the cost of developing and operating AI models.

Also read:

CNA Explains: Why AI leaders are calling for a slowdown – and what makes it so difficult

CHALLENGING BACKDROP FOR AI STOCKS The AI lab comes to the public market just months after SpaceX's record-setting IPO, even as the backdrop for AI stocks has turned more challenging.  Chipmakers and cloud companies central to the business have come under pressure in recent weeks due to valuation concerns, mounting AI infrastructure costs and the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, a key pillar of the industry's growth. The pricing follows a roadshow that attracted demand several times the number of shares offered, Reuters previously reported, despite questions about the company's outlook and its ability to sustain rapid growth as competition in the AI industry intensifies. The company's closest rival, OpenAI, is also expected to pursue a public listing as early as next year. Anthropic's growth has been driven by surging demand for its Claude models, particularly Claude Code, its coding agent that has gained popularity among software developers.  Its annualised revenue run rate reached US$81 billion as of Oct 31, up US$10 billion from Sep 30, according to its IPO filing. The Claude maker said it had 11,900 customers generating at least US$100,000 in annual revenue on a trailing 12-month basis as of Sep 30, compared with more than 1,500 at the end of last year, underscoring its growing business foothold.

Also read:

Commentary: Anthropic’s call for AI development pause deserves attention. It also raises questions

Commentary: Some Anthropic engineers think AI might end us. Why race ahead?

SPENDING COMMITMENTS EXPOSE RISKS But sustaining that growth is becoming expensive. Anthropic spent nearly US$9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, nearly four times the amount spent a year earlier.  It also incurred an additional US$5 billion in computing costs in the third quarter, weighing on efficiency and reducing the revenue generated per dollar of computing capacity. Revenue rose 47 per cent in the third quarter to US$16.96 billion from the second quarter.  The company reported an operating loss of US$567 million, compared with operating income of US$974 million in the previous quarter.  The net loss narrowed to US$23.3 billion from US$66.3 billion a quarter earlier, including non-operating items related to bonds convertible into its shares. Anthropic has committed to nearly US$900 billion in computing spending with infrastructure partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google, part of its ongoing expenditures to train and operate increasingly powerful AI models. Its spending commitments also expose the company to risks beyond its own finances. Anthropic warned in its prospectus that some of its computing providers and infrastructure partners depend on third-party financing and credit support to acquire chips and build capacity. "If such financing or support becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered," Anthropic said in an IPO filing. Investors have grown increasingly concerned about debt-fueled expansion of AI infrastructure, with technology companies and data-centre operators borrowing heavily to finance chips, power and computing facilities. Anthropic also faces questions over how it will balance its commercial ambitions with its emphasis on AI safety.  CEO Dario Amodei has called for the industry to slow the pace of developing and releasing increasingly powerful models, warning that advances in AI could outstrip society's ability to manage the risks.

Also read:

Singapore backs international call for greater frontier AI safeguards

Existing safeguards by AI companies insufficient as models grow more capable: Josephine Teo

COMPETITION AND SAFETY CHALLENGES Competition is intensifying against Anthropic to be the leading provider of AI tools for businesses. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, its latest flagship AI model, accounted for about 13 per cent of enterprise AI spending tracked by corporate expense platform Ramp, compared with about 8 per cent for Anthropic's Claude Fable, according to data cited by Reuters in September.  OpenAI's annualised revenue run rate also passed US$40 billion in July, although Anthropic maintained a lead at the time. The competitive threat extends beyond the handful of companies developing the most powerful commercial models. More large companies are looking to adopt these models, which can be downloaded and run independently, to rein in AI spending. A recent Capgemini study found that 59 per cent of executives at large companies plan to increase their use of open-weight models over the next year as AI costs exceed budgets. Meta Platforms, one of Anthropic's largest customers, has been looking to reduce its use of the startup's models as it develops more AI capabilities internally, Reuters previously reported. "There's going to be other models out there ... Our thesis is that the vast amount of value will accrue to whoever is at the frontier," said Peter Singlehurst, head of private companies at Baillie Gifford, which invested roughly US$1.5 billion in Anthropic before its IPO.  "Our bet is that Anthropic has the ingredients - that doesn't guarantee, but means that they arguably have the highest probability of remaining at the frontier." Anthropic's IPO prospectus warned that its models could develop capabilities faster than the company could evaluate them and put adequate safeguards in place. "Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm," Anthropic said in the filing. The company has said it is considering tighter human oversight of some research and development decisions as its AI models take on a growing share of that work. Shares are expected to start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters for Anthropic's offering, which has a 22-bank underwriting syndicate.  The two banks also served as lead underwriters for SpaceX's IPO earlier this year.

Source: Reuters/rl

Nov 18 : Cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks raised its annual revenue forecast and signed a deal to acquire AI startup Applied Compute in a deal valued at $4.5 billion, as a heightened threat environment pushes customers toward broader security products. Shares of Palo Alto jumped about 10 per cent in after-hours trading to $368.60, and drove gains in rivals. CrowdStrike rose 5.3 per cent, Zscaler climbed 3 per cent and Fortinet gained 2.1 per cent. Palo Alto Networks has been repositioning itself as an integrated cybersecurity provider, with recent deals, including its $3.35 billion acquisition of cloud management and monitoring firm Chronosphere and an agreement with Israeli startup Koi. The company is looking to tap growing cybersecurity spending as the rapid adoption of AI creates new security risks, giving attackers new ways to exploit vulnerabilities.

NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Anthropic's initial public offering is poised to create thousands of paper millionaires among current and former employees, in what could rank among the largest employee wealth windfalls in Silicon Valley history.   The offering is expected to unleash a wave of new wealth across the AI sector, rewarding everyone from early researchers and engineers to administrative staff who received stock grants as the Claude maker raced from startup to one of the world's most valuable companies. The IPO filing shows the amount of wealth embedded in employee stock awards, but not how that wealth is distributed among workers. As a result, outside estimates vary widely. Hill, a San Francisco marketplace for private-company shares, estimates 598 non-founder employees will hold at least $100 million in equity after the initial public offering, which is slated to open on the Nasdaq on Thursday at $83 a share, above its initial target range that would value the company at up to $1.4 trillion, according to a person familiar with the information.

Private-markets research firm Sacra estimates that roughly 2,800 current and former Anthropic employees could hold at least $1 million of pretax vested equity at a $1.35 trillion valuation, the middle of the price range.  The firms say their estimates are model-based and use public information. Reuters could not independently verify the estimates, which reflect factors including vesting periods, exercises, tender transactions, option awards, restricted stock units, award timing, headcount and employee retention rates. The filing does not disclose sums due individuals. But the wealth potentially shared by employees is vast.  Anthropic option holders were sitting on $119 billion of paper gains as of September 30, at a weighted average exercise price of $2.91 per share, the company disclosed. About $73 billion of that amount had vested through service and could be exercised immediately.  Anthropic did not respond to a comment request on the estimates. "The idea of equity appreciating to an amount that is life-changing is something that people strive for," Hill CEO Andrew Benson said. "It doesn't get better than this." EQUITY AT ENTRY LEVEL Workers who joined the firm when it started five years ago —  even in administrative positions and entry-level jobs — could be sitting on life-changing wealth, reflecting their holdings of stock options that carry exercise prices of less than $1.  Options granted through 2023 and still outstanding at the end of that year carried an average exercise price of 52 cents, the filing shows.  At SpaceX, which was founded in 2002 and went  public in June in a record-busting IPO, many of the employees who became millionaires had worked there for more than a decade.    "Early employees who started in a very junior role should have actually a better financial outcome than somebody who joined in a very senior role right before the IPO," Benson said, referring to Anthropic. Non-founder Anthropic employees can sell up to 10 per cent of their holdings on the first trading day, and up to another 35 per cent after fiscal 2026 earnings. EARLY HIRES REAP REWARDS Founded in 2021, the Claude maker expanded its workforce rapidly alongside the AI boom, growing to about 5,300 employees as of September 30 from roughly 940 at the end of 2024. As it hired aggressively, the company used stock-based compensation as a key recruiting tool. A May 2024 job posting for an administrative business partner role shows how the benefits of Anthropic's stock awards extended beyond AI researchers and engineers.  The position, which involved scheduling and managing calendars for company leaders, coordinating conference logistics and handling expense claims and reimbursements, paid an annual salary of $140,000 to $190,000.  The posting added that equity would be "a major component of the total compensation" beyond the salary, indicating that administrative and support staff were also eligible for stock awards alongside cash pay. That year, Anthropic said it granted employees options at an average exercise price of $1.30 per share. "And as we know from several anecdotes after the SpaceX IPO, this is often enough to help people down the organization chart do quite well in IPO," said Marcelo Ballve, head of research at Sacra. Anthropic granted CFO Krishna Rao 14 million stock options in 2024, also with a $1.30 exercise price, according to the filing. At the IPO price range, those options would carry roughly $1 billion in gross intrinsic value, before exercise costs and taxes. Ballve said that equity awards for administrative, support and entry-level roles are not uncommon at venture capital-backed companies. Historically, though, many companies phased out equity grants at hiring for these roles as they scaled up and salaries became more competitive, moving to performance- and tenure-based grants instead. After Anthropic goes public, the company will likely reserve upfront equity grants solely for recruiting top talent, he said.

Nov 18 : Millions of gamers around the world have logged on for the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI," arguably the century's most anticipated video game, offering a glimpse of the vast, interconnected digital infrastructure the global economy increasingly relies on. No major disruption is expected from the rollout. But the scale of demand around one of the gaming industry's biggest releases underscores a broader risk for insurers: a failure at a shared cloud, payments or technology provider could affect thousands of businesses at once. After 13 years in development and an estimated $1 billion or more in production costs, 'Grand Theft Auto VI' began rolling out globally on Thursday, drawing the kind of attention that few entertainment releases ever command. But the fervour also underscores how much modern businesses depend on the digital infrastructure that makes such mass online activity possible, and the risks insurers face when that infrastructure fails.

Insurers cover businesses against financial losses stemming from disruptions to their operations, including some caused by technology failures. As companies increasingly rely on the same cloud providers, payment systems and digital platforms, a single outage could trigger claims from multiple policyholders at once, amplifying exposure. The court said the 18 named companies were not accused of wrongdoing. Many companies have already frozen tokens that were stolen from Binance on October 29 in the largest crypto heist on record. US authorities have attributed the attack to North Korea. “We will continue using every lawful tool available to trace, freeze and recover stolen assets, support our partners in returning funds where possible, and keep those assets out of the hands of the attackers,” Dugan Bliss, deputy general counsel at Binance, said in a statement on Wednesday.

Nov 18 : While the causes of recent disruptions to the way people work, access bank accounts and travel remain unclear, increased efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered vulnerabilities in the AI age are likely a major factor, according to cybersecurity experts and US officials. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking to reporters in Manila this week, said company patching efforts are, at times, "creating short-term disruption in the way the system works." Patches are software and operating system updates intended to fix security vulnerabilities found within a program or product. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told a House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee hearing on worldwide threats Wednesday that there is so far no indication that the tech outages are related. But Clayton said the speed and level of capability of computer systems are "increasing substantially," so legacy computer systems and equipment that already were old are aging much more quickly.

The advent of easily accessible AI tools and large language models has supercharged the discovery of vulnerabilities in software. Microsoft this month has addressed more than 1,200 software vulnerabilities, nearly 20 times higher than in the same month a year ago, according to cybersecurity firm Qualys. At least one major bank was rushing to address a wave of recent patches and there is a lot of work needed, a source at the bank said, speaking on condition of anonymity.  "AI has made finding critical vulnerabilities fast and cheap, and the number of flaws that demand immediate patching has grown with it," said Yuval Itzchakov, CTO and co-founder of autonomous offensive security company A Security.  "Emergency patches go into core infrastructure within hours, often without the full testing cycle, and they are intrusive by design: they change runtimes, kernels and network components that everything else depends on. That speed and scale of change is itself a source of failure," Itzchakov said. Josh Bressers, director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure at cybersecurity firm VulnCheck, said that in 2026 there have been 100,000 publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, tracked by industry as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, or CVEs. Of those, Bressers said, 1,363 were known to have been exploited in the real world.  "Given tight resources for defenders, understanding which vulnerabilities need attention first is critical," Bressers wrote in a LinkedIn post. "Not all vulnerabilities are created equal." Anne Neuberger, general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that AI is helping attackers find and weaponize vulnerabilities, but is a more "valuable friend" to those tasked with defending key computer networks. "AI is enabling enterprises to find 10 times more vulnerabilities," said Neuberger, who served as deputy national security adviser under former President Joe Biden and led incident response to serious national incidents. "And when patching at scale, some can cause problems." Ronald Gestiehr, director of wealth management at Luttner Financial, said technology has made banking "incredibly convenient, and while occasional outages can be frustrating I don't believe the outages will have a significant impact on consumer confidence or change how most people manage their money."  "Financial institutions have invested heavily in technology and security, and, unfortunately, occasional disruptions will happen," Gestiehr said. "What matters most is how quickly those issues are identified, resolved and communicated to customers."

ROME, Nov 18 : A bid for Italy's Avio by Finnish satellite operator Iceye drew a cool initial response from the Italian government, with the defence minister urging state-controlled Leonardo to "think carefully" before selling its stake in the company. On Tuesday Iceye made a €2 billion ($2.2 billion) cash offer for Avio, with the goal of creating an integrated European space and defence group. Defence and aerospace group Leonardo holds a stake of 18 per cent in the rocket maker. The deal, part of a drive to boost European defence integration and reduce reliance on external providers such as Elon Musk's Starshield, will need a green light from the Italian government under its golden power rules to shield strategic assets. However, it remains to be seen whether and under what conditions Rome would clear the operation, as defence-related groups are seen as key to national interest by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who in the past has imposed tight limits on such deals.

Talking to Reuters ahead of a parliament session in Rome, Defence Minister Guido Crosetto - a key ally of Meloni - said Leonardo should be cautious when considering whether to sell its shares to the state-backed Finnish company. "If I were Leonardo, I would think carefully before exiting (Avio)," he said when asked whether part of the shares should remain in Italian hands to protect national interests. SENSITIVE ASSETS This year, the Italian government allowed equity firms Advent and Nextalia to take over Tinexta group on the condition that its defence arm remained in national hands. It was eventually acquired by state lender CDP. Speaking at an event in Helsinki, Iceye CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company had held consultations with the parties involved, including governments, before launching the bid, and that it would take a few more months to close the transaction. However, a person close to the matter told Reuters that Rome had not received any formal notification regarding the Avio bid, and said it was therefore unable to assess it. A second official said the government intended to carry out all the necessary steps to assess the transaction and its implications for the national interest. The offer comes at a particularly sensitive moment for Avio, which is building up capacity in the US market through a new manufacturing plant in Virginia, which it expects to complete in late 2028. In contrast with Crosetto's cautious approach, Leonardo CEO Lorenzo Mariani said on Tuesday that he was "pleasantly surprised" by the bid. A source close to Leonardo said that the group had no contact with Iceye before it launched the bid. A second source said Leonardo would soon hold a board meeting to examine the offer. According to a note published on Wednesday by broker Equita, there was a good chance the deal could proceed, with Leonardo eventually retaining a stake to safeguard Italian presence. Avio shares traded 1.5 per cent higher on Wednesday at €39.75, below the €41 offer price. Nov 18 : Shares of AI-related companies jumped on Wednesday after Nvidia's stronger-than-expected revenue forecast reassured investors about robust AI demand and the chipmaker's outlook following the exit of longtime CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares rose 3.5 per cent in premarket trading after the chipmaker forecast fourth-quarter revenue at $130 billion, plus or minus 3 per cent, above analysts' consensus estimate of $125.25 billion. The company also ruled out rehiring Huang, whose shock exit last week over revelations of extramarital affairs ended three decades of founder-led control. Nvidia has been the centerpiece of the AI trade, supplying the chips that power most AI data centers, and its results are watched as a gauge of demand across the sector.

Under Huang, the company has also financed infrastructure built around its chips, a strategy that has driven demand but also raised questions about circular funding between the chipmaker and its customers. "For Nvidia, strong earnings have bought management time. For the broader AI trade, they reinforce confidence in infrastructure demand, but the next leg of the rally may depend increasingly on which companies can turn that demand into sustainable profits," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. CoreWeave and Nebius Group, neocloud firms backed by Nvidia, jumped 5.4 per cent and 7 per cent, respectively. Data center-related companies Applied Digital, IREN, Core Scientific and Hut 8 also jumped between 5.3 per cent and 6.6 per cent. Chip stocks, widely regarded as among the biggest winners of the AI boom, were broadly higher. Advanced Micro Devices gained 2.9 per cent, Broadcom added 2.9 per cent and Intel climbed 1.8 per cent. Photonic product makers Lumentum and Coherent, along with AI server makers Dell, HPE and Super Micro, gained between 3.2 per cent and 6 per cent each. AI hyperscalers also gained modestly, with Oracle, Alphabet, Amazon.com, Meta Platforms and Microsoft up between 0.4 per cent and 2.8 per cent. Some tech and AI stocks in Japan closed higher, along with an upbeat session for South Korean tech giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The AI trade has also been tested since the Democrats' sweeping wins in the midterm elections stoked fears of tougher regulation of data center buildouts, sending the tech-heavy Nasdaq into correction territory earlier this month. The next test of the AI trade will come as Anthropic prepares to price its public offering later on Wednesday, which could value the company at as much as $1.4 trillion.

NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Meta’s AI agent Muse, embodied by a smiley, fuzzy mascot named Jolly, has burrowed into encrypted personal messages, supplied made-up information about purchases and sent users chats seemingly meant for other people, a fraught start for a bot meant to simplify life for consumers, according to internal company posts reviewed by Reuters. The unbidden actions by Muse – one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads since its September launch, and the centerpiece of Meta’s plan to generate billions of dollars in AI revenue – have prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data, the posts showed. In some of those cases, Meta staffers reported the agent sending them messages about a childcare request they had not made, career advice they had not sought, product orders they had not placed and bank account balances that were not theirs. In one post, from earlier this month, an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post. In another example, an employee using Muse on her personal phone reported it had surprised her with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging service popular with privacy advocates that competes with Meta’s WhatsApp. “This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post.  A colleague responded, saying he had discovered Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system after being similarly caught off guard by unsolicited chats related to apps he had not connected. For this story, Reuters reviewed more than two dozen internal posts describing undesired actions by Muse since its debut, many of them from a feedback group where Meta employees flag problems to the team building the agent. Reuters also worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute, a non-profit that studies AI’s impact on society, to replicate Muse’s access to Signal messages. The results of those tests indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others. In response to questions about Signal access and other Muse safety concerns, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts described the Reuters examples as “isolated incidents,” saying the company prioritizes safety, conducts extensive internal testing and continuously updates products to improve protections. Muse needs to see and interact with people’s computers in order to work on their behalf, and can access other apps only via permissions they explicitly grant, Roberts said. He said many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations, a term referring to AI models’ tendency to make things up, and had already been addressed. Reuters was unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information. DEEP ACCESS The Muse incidents highlight the risks associated with an emerging category of consumer AI agents hitting the market from Meta, OpenAI and others, pitched as the next big wave of AI technology. The bots promise to reshape how digital exchanges operate by executing time-saving tasks like answering emails, booking appointments and making online purchases without direct instructions. Meta is ahead of competitors so far, with Muse consistently topping app download charts after heavy promotion to the company’s more than 3.6 billion users on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. The app’s retention rate is also strong, with around a quarter of the people who have set up Muse accounts returning to use it each day, the company has disclosed. To work effectively, agents need deep access to smartphones and computers. However, they are also prone to making mistakes, exploiting obscure loopholes and accomplishing their objectives in sometimes harmful ways. OpenAI and Anthropic, for instance, have revealed instances of their AI agents unexpectedly hacking other companies and weakening systems designed to monitor their activities.  Some banks and retailers have responded to those risks by blocking agents. The technology is also posing new challenges for operating system providers like Apple and Google, which manage the permissions agents use to navigate around people’s devices. Apple, for instance, changed its operating system this week to give people more control over agents’ data usage after an Inc. Magazine columnist accused Muse of reading private chats from the Messages app on his Mac. Meta has assured Muse users it isolates each agent in its own secure “virtual machine” – a cloud-based emulation of a personal computer – and gives people full control over which apps they connect. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has cited those protections in dismissing calls for industry-wide AI safety standards, arguing companies already have incentives to build safe products, both to earn consumers’ trust and avoid legal risks. Even so, Meta warns incoming users Muse may make mistakes and its terms of service hold users responsible for the agent’s actions.  REPURPOSING SETTINGS To find out how Muse might access encrypted messages without users’ knowledge, Reuters provided a description of the Meta employee’s post – where the bot randomly prompted her to respond to a Signal message – to staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute. Reuters then worked with them to replicate the access she had observed. Testers prompted Muse to read Signal messages on different operating systems. On an Android phone and an Apple laptop, it responded by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead using permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate. Specifically, on Android, it used its permission to access the device's push notifications to retrieve the messages, just as the Meta employees had described. On Apple’s macOS, it used a combination of the computer’s accessibility and screenshot tools, repurposing settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers. The same requests were blocked in tests conducted on an iPhone. The results indicate Meta is interpreting the permissions granted by Muse users broadly, an approach that has long earned the company criticism from privacy advocates and hefty fines from regulators.  In response to Reuters’ findings, Signal President Meredith Whittaker accused Meta of launching Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity,” calling the deployment of agents that can gain wide access to people’s devices “technologically reckless.” She called for app developers like Signal to be given “consistent technical ways” to mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents, for Meta and other AI companies to honor those boundaries and for operating system providers to enforce the rules. Presented with the same findings, Apple and Google said they were considering changes to give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents – though Google, like Meta, noted that people already “must deliberately grant permissions” for apps to access Android notifications. Apple said it had built its accessibility tools for people with disabilities and cautioned that leveraging them “for unintended purposes” could put people’s personal information at risk. Its operating system update this week effectively closed the pathway identified by Reuters, sharply restricting developers’ use of accessibility tools on Macs and introducing a new agent-oriented set of permissions.  “We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said in a statement. ‘NOT MY CONVERSATION’ In other cases discussed internally, staffers reported cases of Muse informing users about transactions that never occurred and making up prices on products they did purchase, costing them real money. In one incident, the agent booked a non-refundable Airbnb stay without permission, an employee reported. Some of the incidents that raised the most concern involved cryptic out-of-context messages sent by the agent that appeared to contain other people’s information, in many cases phrased as replies to queries the users had never submitted.  In a late September social media post, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team behind Muse initially described a user report of a similar problem as a temporary hallucination-related glitch, resolved the same day it arose. However, the internal posts reviewed by Reuters showed such incidents occurring as far back as mid-September and continuing through this month. In one such post, an employee reported his Muse sending him a message “out of nowhere” saying it was unable to submit a request related to a parent’s control over who could access their child’s data. He had done nothing to trigger the chat, and had never discussed child data or caregiving access with his Muse, he said. When he asked Muse about the message, the bot replied: “I don’t have a good explanation for it other than that it wasn’t related to our conversation. Let’s ignore it. How can I help?” Another staffer said Muse randomly offered to “message the seller” about picking up a coffee table. When the employee asked Muse, “What are you talking about?” the agent responded that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.” This was “not my conversation,” the employee said in his post, expressing concern about a “possible cross-account context leak.” To address employee worries, another Superintelligence team member told the internal feedback group in early November that the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions. “These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he said, adding that he was aware of several other cases involving “crypto-related things too, like giving people updates on their Bitcoin balances.” He said the issues involved both the underlying AI model and the software enabling Muse to take actions, and that the team was working through them. Roberts declined to answer Reuters questions about those issues, including how many there were and why they were persisting.

(Additional reporting by Stephen Nellis and Kenrick Cai in San Francisco; Editing by Anna Driver and Ken Li)

WASHINGTON, Nov 18 : NASA's Voyager 1 probe is believed to have now hit a distance milestone accomplished by no other spacecraft from Earth, based on advance computations by the US space agency, as the probe ventures through the near-emptiness of interstellar space. The robotic probe, launched in 1977, was calculated by NASA to have reached a light-day from Earth, the distance that light travels in 24 hours — about 16 billion miles (26 billion km) — on Wednesday at 5:16 a.m. ET (1016 GMT). Officials at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California will have to wait about a day to get a signal from the probe, confirming it has reached this distance. They have scheduled an event for Thursday to discuss the milestone. "Reaching one light-day is an astounding feat, one that I never expected to see," Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd said.

Voyager 1, the most distant human-made object, is flying at almost 38,000 miles per hour (61,000 kph). It crossed the outer edge of the heliosphere, a protective bubble of particles and magnetic fields produced by the sun, to enter interstellar space in 2012. Its twin, Voyager 2, was also launched in 1977 and entered interstellar space in 2018. A Jet Propulsion Laboratory representative said recent power-saving measures could give the two Voyager spacecraft enough power to stay in communication with Earth for three to four more years. "But the goal of the mission is to do science, and there is enough power to keep the current suite of instruments going through the 50th launch anniversary next year. Beyond that is hard to predict, and of course these are nearly 50-year-old spacecraft, and there are always things the team cannot anticipate that might happen," the JPL representative said. Voyager 1 journeyed past Jupiter and Saturn, the solar system's two largest planets, earlier in its mission. It continues to gather scientific data. For instance, its instruments have detected the faint monotonous hum caused by the constant vibrations of the small amounts of gas present in interstellar space. "Voyager is sending back continuous measurements of magnetic fields, cosmic rays and of plasma waves that we receive on Earth whenever the Deep Space Network points its antenna at Voyager," Dodd said. The Deep Space Network is NASA's international array of giant radio antennas supporting interplanetary spacecraft missions. "After the heliopause crossing, the magnetic field direction did not rotate into the interstellar direction as expected, but has maintained the direction it had when both Voyagers crossed the heliopause, a direction governed by our sun. We are watching to see when that rotation might occur," Dodd said. "We also are still observing effects from our sun, including strong solar storms like coronal mass ejections, that generate shocks and pressure fronts that reach as far away as Voyager 1 and beyond," Dodd said. "Where does the sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question."

NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Wall Street, expecting that wealthy investors and retail buyers will battle for shares of Anthropic, is rolling out products tied to the stock, hosting client events and giving away merchandise ahead of the AI company's potentially record launch.  Despite the steep losses among the hyperscalers and other stocks linked to the AI trade in recent weeks, there is building anticipation from these investors for the Anthropic initial public offering, which is expected on Thursday.  The IPO is expected to value the company, which created the Claude chatbot, at up to $1.4 trillion. But it has a hard act to follow after the SpaceX launch, earlier this year, created a frenzy of excitement and events.  "Judging by the number of people interacting with us and asking us about this, and filling out forms, this could be even bigger than SpaceX," said Will Rhind, founder of GraniteShares, who plans to launch a 2x bull Anthropic exchange-traded fund along with a 2x bear product next week.

A successful IPO could boost confidence in other AI-related stocks, including many of the largest technology companies that have powered the stock market rally to a series of record highs, even as shares have recently swung sharply amid questions over the industry's ability to generate measurable profits.  According to industry estimates based on regulatory filings, the market was preparing in coming days for at least 11 leveraged single-stock ETFs from seven issuers, with retail investors accounting for much of the interest.   One advertisement, on the StockTwits investing social media website, read: "Artificial intelligence meets human conviction with the 2X Long Anthropic Daily ETF from Tradr. Coming soon!"  "It’s going to hinge on the bull/bear case for AI," said Rhind. "The believers are not going to be put off by this volatility in the broader AI trade."  Vanda Research, which tracks retail trading activity, said it expects Anthropic itself to attract about $250 million in net retail buying, based on its analysis of activity on listing days and the volume of the company's pre-IPO perpetual futures traded on Hyperliquid. Such a level would double the record $118 million of retail buying for the SpaceX IPO.  Karl Cheong, head of ETFs at Ninepoint Partners in Toronto, points to the selloff in bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies as a sign that retail investors want to raise cash to buy Anthropic. "This will be the first frontier model that retail investors can access easily on a public market," he said. Ninepoint plans to launch an ETF for Canadian investors that would combine leveraged exposure to Anthropic, with a covered call strategy generating income.  WEALTH CLIENTS, LIVESTREAMS, MERCH  Banks have also planned select events. Goldman Sachs organized a launch event on Tuesday for its wealth clients that was attended by the bank's president, John Waldron, as well as Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and its co-founder and president, Daniela Amodei, according to a person familiar with the matter.  JPMorgan plans to livestream the IPO for clients and has prepared merchandise such as t-shirts and laptop covers, according to another person familiar with the matter. Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei and his team were at the bank's offices all day on Friday meeting investors, the person said. Anthropic declined to comment on the two events. Still, not everyone is jumping on the bandwagon.  London-based Ben Preston, responsible for the Orbis Global Equity Strategy, a long-only stock-picking fund which also has a retail investor base, said the fund will not be buying Anthropic at the IPO. “If it comes in at an IPO value of whatever it is – one and a half trillion dollars – that is a very expensive valuation to pay for a company which is unproven," said Preston.  Although StockTwits users give the anticipated IPO an "extremely bullish" score of 85 out of 100, based on a poll on its site, 67 per cent of the more than 18,000 members who responded said they did not plan to buy Anthropic during the initial offering. Only 20 per cent said they will buy, while another 13 per cent said they would wait to see the price.  Some on social media were skeptical about the potential price of the listing. Others said it has been tougher for ordinary investors to get their hands on pre-IPO shares of Anthropic than for SpaceX shares before the latter's IPO in June.  SpaceX has since had a mixed record, with shares priced at $135 in the IPO, jumping to $150 then briefly as high as $225, before dropping as low as $104. They now trade around $142. Still, "as it has gotten closer to (Anthropic's) launch date, I've seen the excitement and the clamor to get a piece of whatever is allocated to retail grow and grow," said Mitchell Caplan, chairman and CEO of Willow Wealth and former CEO of E-Trade Financial.  OVERSEAS INTEREST  Interest has also been building abroad, with many British platforms inviting retail investors to send orders for shares. “Historically, retail investors have been on the sidelines when it comes to public listings," said Jordan Sinclair, president of Robinhood UK. Yet Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, a British investment platform serving high-net-worth investors, said the IPO highlights the divide between connected buyers who can get in pre-IPO and retail investors who end up pleading with their brokers for part of an allocation.  "It's a bit like arriving at a glamorous launch party – institutional backers on the VIP guest list gain early entry, enjoying the vintage champagne and finest canapés behind closed doors," Streeter said in an email. "By the time the doors finally open to the general public, the risk is that the best of the festivities are well underway and latecomers are left paying a steep entry fee to pick over the flat prosecco and leftover crisps."

BEIJING, Nov 18 : Tencent Holdings reported third-quarter revenue growth of 8 per cent on Wednesday, slowing from 11 per cent in the previous quarter as gaming growth cooled, even as demand for artificial intelligence services lifted its cloud business. For the three months ending in September, the Chinese technology giant reported revenue of 207.34 billion yuan ($31.10 billion), falling short of analyst estimates of 210.77 billion yuan, according to LSEG data. Net profit rose 0.8 per cent from the period a year ago to 63.61 billion yuan ($9.54 billion), beating analyst expectations of 59.46 billion yuan. ($1 = 6.6659 Chinese yuan renminbi)
